README.md
Optimizing Acceptance Threshold in Credit Scoring using Reinforcement Learning
The problem environment considered is a trivial credit business process. It starts when the loan provider receives a loan application with the data about the application and the potential borrower. The data is then passed to a credit scoring model that outputs a credit score which reflects the risk level of the loan application.
Next, if the score is too low, the lender rejects the loan application. In case the score is high enough, the lender issues the loan. Eventually, if the loan applicant doesn't repay or defaults on their loan, the lender loses the money. In case the loan applicant repays, the lender gains extra money (from interest and fees).
In the end, any of those cases affect the lender's profits.
Credit business process
Figure 1. Credit business process illustration based on the Credistar Group practice.
In order to make the final accept / reject decision about a loan application, its credit score is compared to an acceptance threshold or cutoff point.
The latter thus regulates the acceptance rates of a credit company and resulting default rates. The problem investigated is the optimization of an acceptance threshold to maximize credit company's profits.
The traditional approach to the problem is to simply optimize the cutoff based on the credit score distribution of an independent test dataset of loan applications. Knowing the outcomes of all the loans in the dataset each possible acceptance threshold is considered and the corresponding profits are calculated.
The optimal cutoff point is the one that corresponds to the maximum profit. In case the train / test split of loan application dataset is random, the acceptance threshold optimized for the test dataset is going to be optimal for the train dataset.
The actual population of loan applications that the credit scoring model is applied to consists of completely new both potentially rejeted and accepted loan applications.
First, we apply the traditional approach to the cutoff point optimization based on the test dataset of loan applications for the credit scoring model. We compute the potential profit for the same range of acceptance threshold values as the action space of the reinforcement learning agent: from 5 to 100 by step of 5.
One can notice that the lower the acceptance threshold, the more loan applications get accepted, the more issued loans default, the bigger the final loss. On the other hand, the higher the acceptance threshold, the less loan applications get accepted, the closer to zero the profit gets.
The optimal acceptance threshold is found by maximizing profit and is equal to a credit score of 65.
Baseline results

results.title: karpatkey (kpk)
results.description:
**karpatkey** (rebranded **[kpk](https://kpk.io/about)** in 2025) is a non-custodial, on-chain manager for DAO treasuries. Most DAO tools answer “where does the money sit” (custody) or “how does a vote move it” (execution); karpatkey answers a different question — *what should an idle treasury actually do*. It is the active-management layer that sits on top of a [Safe](/wiki/dao-governance/tooling/treasury/safe): it designs an allocation strategy, deploys treasury assets into vetted DeFi positions, rebalances them, and reports the results, all without ever holding the DAO's keys. It grew up inside [GnosisDAO](/wiki/daos/networks/gnosisdao), which it was founded in 2021 to serve, and became the reference name for “professional treasury management, done on-chain and non-custodially” ([kpk](https://kpk.io/about)).
## The non-custodial model
The whole design turns on one constraint: the manager must be able to *work* the treasury without being able to *take* it. karpatkey solves this with a proxy **Management [Safe](/wiki/dao-governance/tooling/treasury/safe)** paired with the **[Zodiac](/wiki/dao-governance/tooling/frameworks/zodiac) Roles Modifier** — an open-source module that grants an address a *role*: permission to call only pre-approved functions on pre-approved contracts, with pre-approved parameters. ENS's own mandate describes the setup in exactly those terms — management runs through “a proxy Management Safe and the Zodiac Roles Modifier” ([CoinDesk](https://www.coindesk.com/tech/2022/11/23/ethereum-name-service-selects-karpatkey-dao-as-endaoment-fund-manager)).
In practice the DAO keeps its assets in its own Safe and hands karpatkey a role that can, say, supply to a specific Aave market or add liquidity to a named pool — but *cannot* transfer funds to an outside address, cannot touch unapproved protocols, and can be revoked by the DAO at any time. The manager's discretion is bounded by code, not by trust. This is what “non-custodial” means here: the worst a compromised manager can do is move money between whitelisted DeFi positions, never out the door. It is the same permission-scoping idea that [Zodiac](/wiki/dao-governance/tooling/frameworks/zodiac) brings to governance execution, applied to treasury operations.

Freed from a single mandate, kpk has generalised its playbook into a product: **curated, non-custodial vaults** that apply the same role-scoped, policy-bounded automation to DeFi protocols and, increasingly, to retail depositors — including agent-powered vaults launched on Morpho in late 2025 ([kpk](https://kpk.io/articles/)).

On the [DAO tooling stack](/wiki/dao-governance/tooling/dao-tooling-overview), custody ([Safe](/wiki/dao-governance/tooling/treasury/safe)) and execution ([Zodiac](/wiki/dao-governance/tooling/frameworks/zodiac), on-chain governors) answer where funds live and how a vote moves them. karpatkey occupies the layer above: once the treasury is safely held and governable, *someone still has to decide what to do with it*. For a nine-figure endowment sitting in stablecoins, doing nothing is itself a costly decision — the [treasury-management](/wiki/dao-governance/concepts/treasury/dao-treasury-management) problem of turning a static balance into sustainable runway. karpatkey's contribution is to make that active management delegable without making it custodial, so a DAO can hire professional allocation without handing over the keys. The alternative to hiring that discipline is configuring it: [Enzyme](/wiki/dao-governance/tooling/treasury/enzyme) bakes the same non-custodial, policy-bounded allocation into a self-serve vault contract rather than a managed service.
## How Caper approaches this
karpatkey exists because the mainstream DAO treasury is a [Safe](/wiki/dao-governance/tooling/treasury/safe) that most DAOs don't have the mandate or expertise to actively manage, so they delegate that work to an outside manager and bound the delegation with [Zodiac](/wiki/dao-governance/tooling/frameworks/zodiac) role permissions. A [caper](/wiki/foundations/what-is-a-caper) removes the seam that delegation spans. The treasury is a protocol-controlled vault *inside* the contract, not an external Safe with a manager attached: assets move only through an on-chain [proposal](/wiki/governance/proposals) that members [vote](/wiki/governance/voting) on and that [executes](/wiki/governance/execution) permissionlessly — a `PAYOUT` to fund something or an `INVEST` to deploy capital — with vote weight `(t·v)/(V·T)` combining tokens held and the earned, soulbound record of past voting. There is no manager address to grant a role to, and no discretionary allocation between votes; the same weighting also sets a member's pro-rata share on [exit](/wiki/dao-governance/concepts/membership/rage-quit-and-exit-rights). The trade-off is deliberate and honest: a caper forgoes the professional, actively-managed yield karpatkey delivers in exchange for having no external manager and no custody boundary to trust — every treasury move is a governed, on-chain act by definition. For a treasury that *wants* active DeFi management, karpatkey remains the reference; a caper is the answer for one that wants the treasury and the vote that moves it to be the same thing.

rsETH Incident Report (April 20, 2026)
On 2026-04-18 at 17:35 UTC (Ethereum block 24,908,285), an attacker exploited Kelp’s LayerZero V2 Unichain to Ethereum rsETH route, which was configured as a 1-of-1 DVN. A forged inbound packet from Unichain (srcEid 30320) to Ethereum was verified by a single DVN attestation with no corresponding source-side burn.
From there, the branches followed divergent paths: some supplied rsETH as collateral on Aave V3 on Ethereum, some bridged funds to Arbitrum and opened Aave positions on that chain, and others were routed through different venues.
Aave’s exposure from attacker positions
Of the 116,500 rsETH received by the attacker, 89,567 were deposited on Aave.
Immediate defensive actions taken
Upon identifying the issue, the Aave Protocol Guardian and the Risk Steward coordinated a series of defensive measures to contain risk and protect protocol users.
rsETH and wrsETH freeze
At approximately 19:00 UTC on April 18, the Protocol Guardian began freezing all rsETH and wrsETH reserves across all Aave V3 deployments, setting LTV to 0. New supply and borrowing were disabled, while existing positions remained eligible for repayment and liquidation.
At approximately 14:30 UTC on April 19, the Risk Steward adjusted the WETH interest rate model across Arbitrum, Base, Mantle, and Linea, reducing Slope 2 to 1.50% and bringing the borrow rate at 100% utilization down from 8.5–10.5% to 3.0% APR. This ensured borrow rates remained sustainable under prevailing market conditions.
WETH freeze
At approximately 02:00 UTC on April 20, the Protocol Guardian froze WETH on Core, Prime, Arbitrum, Base, Mantle, and Linea. This action prevented new borrows against WETH collateral and contained the risk of stress spreading to other reserves, including stablecoins.
WETH interest rate adjustment: Core
At approximately 05:00 UTC on April 20, the Risk Steward applied the same interest rate adjustment on Core, with Slope 1 set to 2%, Slope 2 set to 3%, and optimal utilization set to 94%. This ensured borrow rates remained sustainable under prevailing market conditions.
What was not affected
The rsETH bridge exploit on April 18, 2026, was an external event. Aave’s contracts, oracles, and liquidation mechanics functioned as designed throughout, and the protocol’s layered risk framework, Protocol Guardian freezes, and Risk Steward rate adjustments were activated within hours of detection.

## Stablecoin Reserve Strategies: Composition and Rebalancing
Stablecoin reserves are the lifeblood of any DAO treasury. The key is not just holding a single stablecoin but diversifying across issuers and models to mitigate de-pegging risk. Best practice in 2026 splits reserves into three buckets: **fiat-backed** (USDC, USDS) for deep liquidity and regulatory compliance, **crypto-collateralized** (DAI) for decentralization and resilience, and **algorithmic/partially backed** (e.g., FRAX) only in small amounts (≤10% of stablecoin pool).
Rebalancing between stablecoin types should happen automatically when any deviates from its peg by more than 1% for over 6 hours. For example, during the March 2023 USDC de-peg scare, DAOs that auto-converted to DAI avoided losses. Additionally, DAOs should keep at least 6 months of operational expenses in the most liquid stablecoin (typically USDC) with the remainder earning yield in high-quality lending protocols or RWA treasuries.
**Practical tip:** Use a treasury dashboard that monitors stablecoin collateral ratios and alerts the multi-sig signers if any stablecoin falls below its rebalancing threshold. Tools like Zapper, Zerion, or custom Gnosis Safe modules can trigger automatic swaps via 1inch or Cow Swap.

## Risk Framework: Counterparty, Oracle, and Liquidity Risks
Every yield strategy and asset allocation comes with specific risks that must be quantified and capped. **Counterparty risk** applies to centralized issuers (stablecoin issuers, custodians) and lending protocols. Mitigation: diversify across at least three stablecoin issuers, cap exposure to any single protocol at 20% of treasury, and avoid protocols with <500M total value locked at the time of deployment.
**Oracle risk** affects all strategies using price feeds for liquidation or rebalancing. Favor protocols using decentralized oracle networks with multiple sources (Chainlink, Chronicle, Redstone). For critical positions (e.g., collateralized debt positions), use a fallback oracle to prevent manipulation.
**Liquidity risk** arises when the treasury cannot exit a position quickly without significant slippage. DAOs should maintain a “liquidity buffer”—a minimum of 10% of the treasury in instantly redeemable stablecoins. Also, assess the liquidity depth of every pool the treasury participates in; if a $1M swap moves the price by more than 2%, the position is too large for that pool and must be split across venues.
Finally, adopt a **stress test** framework: run scenario simulations (e.g., ETH drops 50%, stablecoin loses peg, lending protocol hacked) quarterly and adjust allocations if any scenario would deplete the operational runway below 12 months.

The safest are lending on Aave or Compound (variable rates), depositing into sDAI (Savings DAI), or buying short-term tokenized US Treasury bills via Ondo Finance or similar. All three offer 4-8% APY historically with minimal additional risk beyond protocol risk.

results.title: Stablecoin Depeg Risk for Treasury
results.description:
- A stablecoin can trade below par under stress. USDC/SVB is the clearest precedent: a portion of reserves at one bank, brief sub-$1 trading until access was resolved.
- Drivers: reserve quality and counterparty/banking concentration, amplified by opacity and market panic.
- Diversification through per-issuer limits is the single most effective treasury control — it caps the damage regardless of which issuer fails.
- The depeg contingency playbook must be pre-decided: detection, decision rights, actions, recording.
- GENIUS and MiCA reduce but do not remove depeg risk — a mitigant, not a guarantee.
- This pairs with the [stablecoin treasury policy](/blog/stablecoin-treasury-policy) (which sets the limits) and [reserve transparency](/blog/stablecoin-reserve-transparency-attestation).
## The peg is not unconditional
The instructive precedent: around the Silicon Valley Bank failure, a portion of USDC's reserves was held at the bank, and USDC traded below one dollar briefly until access concerns were resolved. The lesson is not that a specific stablecoin is unsafe — it is that a reserve or counterparty problem can break a peg even for a well-regarded coin. A treasury that assumes the peg is unconditional has an unmanaged risk.
## What drives depeg risk
- reserve quality — which assets back the coin, and how liquid and high-quality they are;
- counterparty and banking concentration — where the reserves are held;
- opacity — whether holders can quickly verify backing during stress;
- market panic — confidence can break before fundamentals do.
It is an issuer-and-reserves question (see [reserve transparency](/blog/stablecoin-reserve-transparency-attestation)), not a generic "crypto is volatile" one.
## Diversification caps the damage
The single most effective treasury-level control is per-issuer concentration limits. They ensure no single issuer's depeg or freeze hits the entire position, turning a potential total liquidity loss into a bounded, survivable one. Diversification does not prevent a depeg — it caps the damage from any one, which is why it works regardless of which issuer has the problem (the [policy](/blog/stablecoin-treasury-policy) control made concrete).
## The contingency playbook
Pre-decided, because a depeg is fast:
| Element | Decide in advance |
|---|---|
| **Detection** | Price thresholds, reserve-event news triggers |
| **Authority** | Who is authorised to act |
| **Actions** | Rotate issuer, redeem, hedge, pause stablecoin usage |
| **Order** | Sequence of operations |
| **Recording** | Event + decisions in the [audit trail](/blog/crypto-audit-trail-piste-fiable) |
Improvising during a depeg is how treasuries take avoidable losses. Decide while calm.
## Regulation reduces, does not remove
US [GENIUS](/blog/genius-act-stablecoin-treasury-impact) and EU [MiCA](/blog/mica-stablecoins-art-emt) raise the floor on reserve quality and transparency for compliant issuers, lowering depeg probability but not to zero. A treasury still needs diversification and a contingency plan. Regulation is a mitigant, not a guarantee, and it is jurisdiction-specific.

**Monitoring infrastructure:**
- Designate a specific team member (or rotation) responsible for daily stablecoin price monitoring. In normal conditions this is a one-minute task; during stress events it becomes the most time-sensitive item on the treasury agenda.
- Set up price-threshold alerts for every held stablecoin issuer. The threshold should be below normal market noise (brief $0.001 intraday fluctuations are not depeg signals) but well above the point of serious concern. A common approach: alert at $0.995, escalate at $0.99, invoke contingency below $0.97.
- Subscribe to issuer reserve and operational communications channels. A banking counterparty issue or regulatory development at an issuer will often be publicly observable before the price reflects it.

**Contingency playbook testing:**
- At least once per year, run a tabletop exercise: a scenario where one held stablecoin begins depegging during business hours. Walk through every step of the playbook: who gets notified, who makes the call, which system is used to execute the rotation, how the accounting entry is recorded, and how the board is notified. Identify gaps.
- After the exercise, update the playbook to address the gaps found, and re-file the updated version.
## Accounting treatment for depeg events
A depeg event has specific accounting consequences that must be handled correctly, not deferred or averaged away:
- **During the depeg (while holding the affected stablecoin)**: the holding is measured at its current market value, not its nominal $1.00 peg. If the functional currency is USD and the stablecoin is trading at $0.96, the holding is worth $0.96 per token. An unrealised measurement loss is recognised per the applicable framework.
- **On disposal during a depeg (rotation or redemption at below-peg price)**: the realised loss is the difference between the carrying value at disposal and the proceeds received. This is a distinct accounting entry from the pre-depeg holding.
- **Recovery to peg after a temporary depeg**: if the stablecoin returns to $1.00 and the holding was not disposed of, the prior unrealised loss is reversed. Under fair-value accounting (where applicable), the position reverts to the recovered price. Confirm the reversal treatment with your accountant — it is framework-specific.
- **Classification review**: a stablecoin that has experienced a material depeg event, even temporarily, warrants a reclassification review — re-examine whether it remains appropriate to classify it close to cash, or whether its instrument risk has changed the appropriate balance-sheet line.
## Practical guidance
1. **Reject "it's a dollar"** — the peg is conditional (USDC/SVB precedent).
2. **Assess reserve quality and banking concentration** per issuer.
3. **Enforce per-issuer diversification limits** — the damage cap.
4. **Pre-decide the depeg playbook** — triggers, authority, actions, order, recording.
5. **Treat GENIUS/MiCA as mitigants**, not guarantees.
6. **Record depeg events and decisions** in the audit trail; confirm approach with advisers.

results.title: How to Design a Treasury Stress Testing Process
results.description:
On-chain treasuries require **multivariate scenario modeling** because DeFi risks compound. A stablecoin depeg (like USDC dropping to $0.87 during the March 2023 banking crisis) can trigger cascading liquidations in lending markets where that stablecoin serves as collateral, which in turn forces protocol-owned liquidity positions out of range, generating impermanent loss while governance tokens simultaneously crash. Each risk vector amplifies the others.

Building the simulation pipeline starts with **risk factor identification and correlation mapping**. Enumerate every protocol where treasury funds are deposited, every token held, every smart contract with spending authority, and every governance parameter that controls fund movement. For each, define shock magnitudes based on historical precedents: stablecoin depegs of 10-90%, protocol hacks resulting in 30-100% loss of deposited funds, governance token price drawdowns of 50-95%, and timelock bypass scenarios where malicious proposals execute within hours instead of days. Correlation assumptions matter more than individual shock magnitudes because simultaneous failures drive tail risk.

| Scenario Type | Severity 1 (Moderate) | Severity 2 (Severe) | Severity 3 (Critical) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Market Crash | 20-30% drawdown in majors; stablecoins hold peg | 40-60% drawdown; one major stablecoin depegs below $0.95 | 70%+ drawdown; multiple stablecoins lose peg; liquidity freezes |
| Stablecoin Depeg | Minor deviation (0.98-0.99); arbitrage restores within hours | Sustained depeg (0.90-0.95); redemption queues form; 24h+ recovery | Catastrophic depeg (<0.80); bank run; permanent capital loss likely |
| Protocol Exploit | Isolated contract bug; <5% of treasury at risk; patch available |

## Defining Acceptable Loss Thresholds and Risk Limits
Mapping simulation outputs to governance-actionable risk limits across asset categories
| Risk Parameter | Stablecoin Allocation | Native Token Holdings | DeFi Yield Positions |
|---|---|---|---|
| Maximum Drawdown Limit | 2% of stablecoin NAV | 25% from peak valuation | 15% of position value |
| Runway Preservation Floor | 18 months operating expenses | 6 months minimum runway | 12 months coverage buffer |
| Concentration Limit | 80% single stablecoin cap | 40% of total treasury | 10% per protocol |
| Liquidation Threshold | None (full redemption) | 5% daily volume ceiling | 72-hour exit window |
| Rehypothecation Cap | 0% (no lending) | 10% of native supply | 30% of yield portfolio |
| Correlation Buffer | 1.0 peg deviation tolerance | 0.7 beta to ETH maximum | 0.5 cross-protocol correlation |
| Recovery Trigger | Automatic stable swap at 0.98 | TWAP below 200-day MA | Audit failure or admin key change |

## Building the Contingency Response Playbook
Translating stress test results into executable response procedures with defined triggers, pre-authorized actions, and fallback paths.
Stress testing reveals where a treasury breaks. A contingency response playbook converts those failure points into **pre-authorized action sequences** that execute without requiring real-time governance votes during a crisis. The core principle is simple: if signers need to debate thresholds while a stablecoin depegs, the treasury has already lost. Each playbook entry must define a **trigger condition**, the **authorized response**, the **execution path**, and the **fallback procedure** when primary paths fail.
Trigger conditions must be unambiguous and machine-verifiable where possible. A trigger like "market downturn" is useless. Instead, define specific thresholds: *"ETH drops below $1,800 on a 30-day TWAP basis"* or *"USDC trades below $0.97 for more than 4 consecutive hours on CoinGecko."* For protocol hacks, triggers include on-chain events such as unexpected `owner` transfers, large outflows from known treasury addresses, or anomaly detection alerts from services like [Forta](https://forta.org) or [Chaos Labs](https://chaoslabs.xyz). Each trigger should map to a **severity level** that determines which playbook activates.
## Escalation Levels and Loss Thresholds
A practical playbook uses three escalation tiers tied to potential loss magnitude. **Level 1 (Minor)** covers events with less than 5% treasury impact: a single signer key compromise, a minor stablecoin deviation, or an isolated protocol exploit with limited exposure. Response: rotate the affected signer, withdraw from the affected protocol, notify the committee. **Level 2 (Significant)** covers 5-20% impact: a major stablecoin depeg, a critical smart contract vulnerability in a treasury module, or coordinated governance attack attempts. Response: activate timelock bypass, execute pre-signed withdrawal transactions, move affected assets to cold storage. **Level 3 (Critical)** covers 20%+ impact: protocol hacks draining core treasury contracts, catastrophic oracle manipulation, or L1 consensus failures. Response: execute emergency shutdown procedures, activate all guardian powers, coordinate out-of-band with exchange partners to freeze bridged assets.

Stress testing models **tail-risk events** like a 50% drawdown in ETH within 24 hours, a major stablecoin depegging to $0.85, or a protocol hack draining 30% of deployed capital.

results.title: 10 Treasury Stress Tests Your DAO Needs Quarterly
results.description:
Here’s the architecture I’ve seen work without becoming a risk-theater circus:
```
[Wallets + Custodians + LP Positions] [Market Data + Oracles] | | +----------> [Treasury Canon] <-----+ (clean positions) | v [Scenario Engine / Models] (haircuts, correlations, shocks) | v [Risk Dashboard + Alerts] | v [Pre-approved Governance Actions] (rebalance, unwind, hedge, pause, cap exposure)
```
Now the tests.
## 1) Stablecoin depeg + redemption freeze test
## What you simulate
A “safe” stablecoin trades at **$0.86–$0.95** for 3–10 days *and* redemptions are delayed or operationally constrained.
## Why it matters
Even “fully reserved” stables have real-world linkages. The USDC depeg in March 2023 is the canonical reminder that **reserve location + banking rails** can matter as much as on-chain liquidity.
## How to run it (quick)
- Apply haircuts by stable type:
- fiat-backed: -5% to -15%
- crypto-backed: -10% to -25%
- algorithmic: treat as “can go to zero” (sorry)
- Add a constraint: “only X% redeemable per day”
- Recompute runway + obligations coverage
## What you’re looking for
- Can you fund operations for 6–12 months without forced selling?
- Do you have stablecoin concentration risk (single issuer, single chain)?

## 3) 50% market drawdown + correlation spike test
## What you simulate
A classic crypto tantrum: majors drop 40%–60% and correlations converge toward 1.
## Why it matters
Diversification often disappears precisely when you need it. A treasury split across “10 tokens” might still be one trade: **risk-on crypto beta**.
## How to run it
- Apply drawdowns by bucket (majors, long tail, governance tokens)
- Increase correlations in your model (or simply shock everything together)
- Recalculate: runway, vote-controlled liabilities, and min-stable thresholds

```
import pandas as pd # treasury.csv columns: asset, bucket, usd_value df = pd.read_csv("treasury.csv") # Define scenario haircuts (negative = loss) SCENARIOS = { "stable_depeg": {"stable": -0.10, "majors": -0.35, "long_tail": -0.55}, "risk_off": {"stable": -0.02, "majors": -0.50, "long_tail": -0.70}, "lst_discount": {"stable": -0.02, "majors": -0.40, "long_tail": -0.60, "lst": -0.08}, } def run_scenario(df, scenario): haircuts = SCENARIOS[scenario] stressed = df.copy() stressed["haircut"] = stressed["bucket"].map(haircuts).fillna(0.0) stressed["stressed_value"] = stressed["usd_value"] * (1.0 + stressed["haircut"]) return stressed scenario_name = "stable_depeg" out = run_scenario(df, scenario_name) summary = out.groupby("bucket")[["usd_value","stressed_value"]].sum() summary["loss"] = summary["stressed_value"] - summary["usd_value"] print(f"\nScenario: {scenario_name}") print(summary.sort_values("loss")) print("\nTotal stressed value:", out["stressed_value"].sum())
```

Turn outputs into **governance-ready policies**:
- exposure caps by asset + venue
- minimum stable runway (e.g., 9–12 months)
- automatic rebalance bands
- approved unwind paths for risky yield
- an emergency playbook that isn’t written during the emergency

results.title: DAO Treasury Management 2026: Stablecoins, Diversification Guide
results.description:
DAO treasuries collectively hold tens of billions of dollars of crypto assets — and most of them are catastrophically misallocated. The dominant pattern is a treasury that is 70-95% concentrated in the DAO's own governance token, with the remainder split between ETH and a small stablecoin reserve. This structure is a recipe for ruin: when the native token price drops, the treasury shrinks in parallel, often exactly when the DAO most needs runway to execute through the drawdown. This guide explains the specific risks, the diversification frameworks mature DAOs use, and how on-chain treasury operations are structured in 2026.

## The Native Token Concentration Problem
If a DAO holds $100M of treasury — 90% in its native token, 10% in stablecoins — and the token drops 80%, the treasury is now $18M in native tokens plus $10M in stablecoins, for $28M total. That's a 72% drawdown in treasury value during a period when the DAO almost certainly needs to spend more on stabilizing the protocol and rebuilding confidence. The native token allocation that looked like aligned incentive in good times becomes the existential risk in bad times.
Public DAO treasury reports show this pattern repeatedly. Tokens like LUNA, FTT, and dozens of smaller projects either collapsed or saw treasuries decimated when their native token followed the broader market into 80-95% drawdowns. Even DAOs whose tokens recovered spent multi-year periods with limited operating runway during the trough.
## The Diversification Framework
| Asset Category | Target Allocation Range | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Native governance token | 30-60% | Alignment, governance signal, protocol upside |
| Stablecoins (USDC, USDT, DAI, etc.) | 20-40% | Operating runway, predictable expenses |
| Tokenized money market funds | 0-15% | Yield-bearing stablecoin replacement |
| ETH / BTC (blue chip crypto) | 5-15% | Uncorrelated crypto exposure, large-cap liquidity |
| Ecosystem stable yield (Aave, Spark, Sky) | 5-15% | Yield on stablecoin allocation |
| Strategic illiquid positions | 0-10% | Partnerships, equity, real-world assets |
## Stablecoin Allocation Mechanics
Stablecoin allocation is the single most consequential treasury decision. A reasonable benchmark is 2-4 years of operating expenses in stablecoins regardless of native token performance. For a DAO with $5M annual expenses, that's $10-20M in stablecoins. Mature DAOs (Optimism Foundation, Arbitrum Foundation, Uniswap, ENS) maintain substantial stablecoin balances precisely because their experience says native-token-heavy treasuries are fragile.
Within the stablecoin allocation, diversification matters too. Single-issuer concentration creates issuer risk (Silicon Valley Bank's failure briefly depegged USDC; Tether has its own ongoing counterparty considerations). A diversified stablecoin allocation might hold USDC, USDT, DAI, and increasingly tokenized money market funds like [BlackRock BUIDL or Ondo USDY](/en/blog/tokenized-money-market-funds-blackrock-buidl-2026) for yield-bearing replacement. [Best stablecoins for trading](/en/blog/best-stablecoins-for-trading-2026) covers the issuer-by-issuer detail.

Selling treasury tokens to public DEXs is operationally simple but practically catastrophic at any meaningful size — the DAO's own selling crashes its token. Three better channels:
- **OTC desks** — Bilateral conversion of native tokens to stablecoins at negotiated prices, settled off-mempool. The dominant institutional channel for size
- **Token swaps with strategic partners** — Cross-treasury swaps between aligned DAOs/protocols; sometimes structured as long-term commitments
- **Structured products / TWAP** — Algorithmic execution over weeks or months, typically through OTC counterparties offering structured liquidity
Mintarex's [OTC service](/en/otc) handles exactly this profile of trade — large bilateral conversions across 500+ assets, settlement under 10 minutes, deep stablecoin liquidity, and 6 fiat currencies for organizations needing the diversification to extend into traditional finance treasury. For DAO foundations operating across jurisdictions, the [institutional service](/en/institutional) supports the compliance and reporting workflows typical of governance-mandated treasury operations.
Reality Check
DAO governance proposals to sell 5%+ of native token treasury into stablecoins are almost always controversial. Token holders see them as bearish signals. The arithmetic argument — that diversification protects future operations from token volatility — runs into the reflexive argument — that selling signals lack of conviction. Mature DAOs frame these proposals as risk management, not directional bets, and execute through channels that minimize visible market impact.

Common benchmarks: enough stablecoins to cover 2-4 years of operating expenses regardless of native token price. For a DAO with $5M annual operating expenses, that means $10-20M in stablecoins. Many mature DAOs (Optimism Foundation, Arbitrum Foundation, Uniswap, ENS) hold substantial stablecoin allocations alongside their native tokens. The specific ratio depends on burn rate, native token liquidity, and the DAO's risk policy — but having less than one year of stablecoin runway is a known failure pattern.

results.title: Stablecoin Treasury Policy
results.description:
Holding stablecoins on treasury without a written policy is an unmanaged risk. A policy sets which stablecoins qualify, concentration limits per issuer, the issuer/reserve due-diligence test, and the depeg contingency plan — operational decisions, distinct from which asset 'wins' a comparison.

Most stablecoin treasury losses are not bad asset picks — they are the absence of a policy: everything in one issuer, no due-diligence cadence, no plan for a depeg. This is the hub document for the stablecoin sub-cluster: the written policy that the asset comparison, the GENIUS explainer, the depeg-risk article, and the reserve-transparency guide all feed into. It is deliberately not a comparison and not a regulatory recap — it is the durable framework that turns those inputs into rules a treasury actually operates by: eligibility, concentration limits, recurring due diligence, and the depeg contingency.
## What the policy comes down to
- A written policy beats picking "the best" stablecoin: it is durable governance, not a point-in-time call.
- Components: eligibility, concentration limits (per issuer and in aggregate), issuer/reserve due diligence, custody rules, and a depeg contingency.
- Concentration limits are the core control, because single-issuer concentration is the dominant risk.
- Due diligence is recurring, since issuer status and reserves change (track against [GENIUS](/blog/genius-act-stablecoin-treasury-impact) and [MiCA](/blog/mica-stablecoins-art-emt)).
- The depeg contingency is pre-decided — settled in calm conditions, not mid-stress.
- This is distinct from the [asset comparison](/blog/usdc-vs-usdt-vs-dai-treasury): that comparison informs eligibility, while the policy governs behaviour.

## The components
| Component | What it sets |
|---|---|
| Eligibility | Which stablecoins may be held, and why |
| Concentration limits | Max exposure per issuer and in aggregate |
| Issuer/reserve due diligence | Issuer status, reserve composition/quality, transparency cadence |
| Custody rules | Multisig, role-based access (see [treasury policy controls](/blog/multisig-treasury-policy-controls)) |
| Depeg contingency | Triggers, decision rights, actions, recording |
This is an operational governance document, not a market opinion.
## Concentration limits: the core control
Single-issuer concentration is the dominant stablecoin treasury risk. A depeg, freeze, or issuer failure hits the whole position if it is all in one stablecoin. Concentration limits — caps per issuer and in aggregate — convert a binary catastrophic exposure into a bounded, survivable one. The limit is the control; which stablecoins you hold is secondary to not over-concentrating in any. This is the [diversification](/blog/stablecoin-depeg-risk-treasury) discipline written as a hard policy rule.
## Issuer and reserve due diligence
The test is recurring, not one-off:
- issuer regulatory status — a permitted payment stablecoin issuer under [GENIUS](/blog/genius-act-stablecoin-treasury-impact)? MiCA-compliant ([EMT/ART](/blog/mica-stablecoins-art-emt))?
- reserve composition and quality — cash and short Treasuries versus riskier assets;
- transparency cadence — monthly disclosure plus an independent audit, not only a [proof-of-reserves](/blog/stablecoin-reserve-transparency-attestation) dashboard;
- operational controls at the issuer.
Issuer practices and status change, so diligence is a cadence, not a checkbox.
## The depeg contingency plan
A pre-decided playbook for a held stablecoin losing its peg:
- detection triggers and thresholds;
- who decides;
- the actions available: rotate, redeem, hedge, halt usage;
- how the event is recorded (the [audit trail](/blog/crypto-audit-trail-piste-fiable)).
Decide under calm conditions. A treasury without a depeg plan improvises exactly when improvisation is most costly (see [stablecoin depeg risk](/blog/stablecoin-depeg-risk-treasury)).

- Write the depeg playbook as a decision tree, not a narrative: "if spot price falls below $0.97 for more than 2 hours, the treasury lead is authorised to rotate up to 100% of the affected issuer's holding to nominated alternative; if spot price falls below $0.95, halt any new stablecoin-denominated payments pending board notification."

- **Depeg event handling**: when the contingency plan is activated, the accounting records the rotate/redeem/hedge action at the actual transacted value. Any realized loss from disposing of a depegged holding is recognized at the transaction price, not at the pre-depeg assumed peg. The depeg event, the decision, and the action are all recorded in the audit trail.

## Practical guidance
1. **Write the policy** — eligibility, limits, due diligence, custody, contingency.
2. **Make concentration limits hard rules** — per issuer and aggregate.
3. **Run recurring issuer/reserve due diligence** — status changes.
4. **Pre-decide the depeg playbook** — triggers, decision rights, actions.
5. **Keep the policy distinct from the asset pick** — the pick feeds eligibility.
6. **Record policy adherence** in the audit trail; confirm with advisers.

Writing the policy — eligibility, limits, the depeg playbook — is the treasury's call, and a legal/treasury adviser's to sign off. What [Wag3s Ledger](/ledger) does is make it measurable: it tags stablecoin holdings by issuer, reports per-issuer and aggregate concentration against your policy limits, and keeps the audit trail of policy adherence and depeg-event handling, so the policy is enforced and evidenced rather than just filed.

results.title: MakerDAO Weighs Using Emergency Switch to Prevent Future DAI Depegging
results.description:
Finance
MakerDAO Weighs Using Emergency Switch to Prevent Future DAI Depegging
The community proposal comes just two days after DAI followed stablecoin USDC in slipping beneath the one-dollar mark.
The community behind MakerDAO, the issuer of the $6.3 billion market cap DAI stablecoin, is considering emergency measures to protect DAI from slipping beneath the dollar mark as a nationwide banking crisis threatens crypto.
Under the proposal, the community would adopt an emergency switch that would pause peg-stability-module (PSM) swaps on its protocol, freezing the token purchases required to mint new DAI tokens, Sam MacPherson, a protocol engineer at MakerDAO, told CoinDesk.
“That [PSM pause] would prevent DAI from following the price of any depegging stablecoin,” MacPherson said.
The proposal comes just two days after DAI, a so-called decentralized stablecoin backed by many assets including USDC, fell to an all-time low of 88 cents.
DAI’s depegging occurred after Circle, the issuer of USD coin USDC $1.0001 , revealed it had billions of dollars of its stablecoin’s collateral at the failed Silicon Valley Bank, sending the price of USDC tumbling. On Monday, USDC regained its dollar peg .
DAI’s reliance on USDC for roughly 52% percent of its reserves rendered it vulnerable to losing its dollar peg. The protocol uses PSM swaps, a vault that permits users to “swap a given collateral type directly for DAI at a fixed rate, rather than borrowing DAI,” according to MakerDAO .
The emergency measure would allow the protocol to circumvent its normal 16-hour waiting period, which was already shortened from two days, on freezing PSM swaps, intended to allow DAI’s issuer to act swiftly enough to prevent the token’s price from following in the same direction as other stablecoins such as USDC.
It's not clear how much time it would take for DAI to begin depegging if one of the tokens by which it is collateralized starts depegging.
The pause switch for PSM swaps isn’t automatically triggered when one of the assets that backs DAI begins depegging, so the MakerDAO community would have to vote to use the tool.
“The TLDR is that an emergency switch is being added to pause PSM swaps. Normally there is a two-day delay on any action, so this bypasses that delay,” MacPherson said in a Telegram message. “It’s not being planned to be used, but it’s there if governance needs.”

USDC's Depeg Laid Bare the Risks Traditional Finance Poses to Stablecoins
A Moody's analyst examines how the recent banking crisis spilled into crypto, and why alternatives to stablecoins such as tokenized bank deposits and CBDCs may be needed to prevent contagion.

What Is Inventory Risk in Crypto Market Making?
Inventory risk arises because market makers need to hold cryptocurrency assets for trading and liquidity provisioning. If the market moves in only one direction, market makers face the risk of losing value in an unbalanced position.
For instance, if a crypto market maker accumulates a sizeable long position during a price decline, the market maker runs the risk of incurring substantial losses on that inventory.
However, exposure to these price fluctuations can be reduced by trading across exchanges or offsetting positions in derivatives markets.
Managing risk exposure is a key part of crypto market making services because it helps the market stay stable and its participants to make money. To protect themselves from various risks, crypto market makers use different hedging strategies, specifically targeting the risks of holding inventory while quoting buy and sell prices.
These methods are designed to quote buy and sell prices while managing the risk of holding volatile inventory.
Let’s dive deeper into the most common hedging strategies in crypto market making to uncover how they work in practice.
Many crypto market makers use derivatives such as crypto options and perpetual futures to protect their investments; in other words, to hedge.
This is a common way for a crypto market maker to hedge inventory on crypto exchanges, especially since many well-known tokens also have developed futures markets.
At the same time, crypto options trading gives market makers and institutional players another way to protect themselves from big price changes.
On the other hand, market makers can hedge short positions using call options or other option structures. The ongoing growth of the crypto option market throughout 2024 has expanded the toolset for risk management, allowing market makers to hedge with greater nuance in volatile markets.
This type of trading hedges the position right away, neutralising inventory accumulation. If done correctly, the market maker makes a small spread on the less liquid venue while removing directional risk on the liquid venue.
In addition to external hedging instruments, crypto market makers usually manage inventory risk by dynamically adjusting their bid and ask price quotes in what is called Dynamic Inventory Management .
If the inventory becomes unbalanced, a market maker modifies its quotes to encourage trading in the direction that will rebalance it.

results.description:
- Brier Skill Score is a metric that evaluates probabilistic forecasts by comparing predicted probabilities with observed outcomes against a climatological baseline.
- It decomposes mean forecast error into reliability, resolution, and uncertainty, providing insight into forecast calibration and practical model improvements.
- BSS is applied in operational settings such as solar flare prediction, where enhanced calibration and bias correction optimize decision thresholds and risk analysis.
The Brier Skill Score (BSS) is a quantitative metric for evaluating the performance of probabilistic forecasts relative to a reference forecast, typically climatology. BSS is widely used in the verification of event probability forecasts—such as solar flare prediction—to quantify gains in forecast accuracy and reliability versus a naïve, frequency-based baseline. By construction, BSS provides a standardized, skill-relative evaluation that decomposes mean probabilistic forecast error into contributions from calibration (reliability), forecast sharpness (resolution), and intrinsic climatological uncertainty. Major reference treatments of BSS in operational probabilistic verification include Nishizuka et al. (2020) and Leka et al. (2018) ([Nishizuka et al., 2020](/papers/2007.02564), &&&[1](https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/u-1-dirac-spin-liquid)&&&).

## 2. Decomposition: Reliability, Resolution, and Uncertainty

Calibration or reliability is a key requirement on any probability forecast or probabilistic classifier. In a nutshell, a probabilistic classifier assigns a predictive probability to a binary event. The classifier is calibrated or reliable if, when looking back at a series of extant forecasts, the conditional event frequencies match the predictive probabilities. For example, if we consider all cases with a predictive probability of about 0.80, the observed event frequency ought to be about 0.80 as well.

The key diagnostic tool for checking calibration is the reliability diagram, which plots the observed event frequency against the predictive probability. In discrete settings, where there are only a few predictive probabilities, such as, e.g., 0,110,…,910,1, this is straightforward. However, even in discrete settings, there might be many such values. Furthermore, statistical and machine-learning approaches to binary classification generate continuous predictive probabilities that can take any value between zero and one, and typically the forecast values are pairwise distinct. In these settings, researchers have been using the “binning and counting” approach, which starts by selecting a certain, typically arbitrary, number of bins for the forecast values. results.title: The Brier Score for Probability Forecasts
results.description:
The Brier score is just the mean squared error between your predicted probability and the 0/1 outcome. Lower is better, it is bounded between 0 and 1, and it punishes both miscalibration (wrong probabilities) and indecision (probabilities stuck near the base rate) at the same time.
## What the Brier Score Measures
For a set of N binary events, let p_i be the predicted probability of the event and y_i \in \{0, 1\} the observed outcome. The Brier score is the average squared difference between them:
BS = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} (p_i - y_i)^2
If you forecast 0.9 and the event happens (y = 1), you pay a tiny penalty of (0.9 - 1)^2 = 0.01. If you confidently forecast 0.9 and the event does *not* happen, you pay (0.9 - 0)^2 = 0.81. That asymmetry is the whole point: confident-but-wrong predictions are expensive, so the score pressures you to report probabilities you actually believe.
### A Proper Scoring Rule
The Brier score is a **proper scoring rule**, meaning your expected score is minimized only when you report your true belief about the probability. There is no clever way to game it by shading your numbers toward 0 or 1. This is the same property that makes [log loss a defensible alternative](/blogs/brier-score-vs-log-loss-vs-calibration/); both reward honesty, but they distribute their penalties differently.
## Brier Score vs Accuracy
Accuracy throws away information. It first rounds every probability to a hard 0 or 1 at some threshold, then asks only whether the label matched. A forecaster that says 0.51 and one that says 0.99 are treated identically when both are correct, even though one is far more useful. The Brier score keeps the full resolution of the probability, which is why probabilistic models should be graded with it.
| Metric | Range | Uses probability? | Rewards calibration? | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Accuracy | 0 to 1 (higher better) | No (thresholded) | No | Final hard decisions |
| Brier score | 0 to 1 (lower better) | Yes | Yes | Probability forecasts |
| Log loss | 0 to ∞ (lower better) | Yes | Yes | Penalizing overconfidence |
| AUC / ROC | 0.5 to 1 (higher better) | Ranking only | No | Discrimination / ranking |

## The Murphy Decomposition
The most illuminating property of the Brier score is that it splits cleanly into three interpretable pieces. Group the predictions into K bins by their forecast value, and let n_k be the count in bin k, \bar{p}_k the mean prediction in that bin, \bar{o}_k the observed event rate in that bin, and \bar{o} the overall base rate. Murphy's identity is:
BS = \underbrace{\frac{1}{N}\sum_k n_k (\bar{p}_k - \bar{o}_k)^2}_{\text{reliability}} - \underbrace{\frac{1}{N}\sum_k n_k (\bar{o}_k - \bar{o})^2}_{\text{resolution}} + \underbrace{\bar{o}(1 - \bar{o})}_{\text{uncertainty}}
- **Reliability (lower is better)** — how far the predicted probabilities drift from the observed frequencies. This is the *calibration* term. A perfectly calibrated forecaster has reliability of zero.
- **Resolution (higher is better)** — how much the forecaster's bins separate high-risk from low-risk events. A model that always predicts the base rate has zero resolution and adds no value.
- **Uncertainty (fixed)** — the irreducible variance of the outcome itself, \bar{o}(1 - \bar{o}). No model can change it; it sets the difficulty of the problem.
> **Pro tip:** Because the score is reliability minus resolution plus a fixed uncertainty, two models with the same Brier score can be very different. One might be beautifully calibrated but indecisive (low reliability, low resolution); the other sharp but biased (high resolution, high reliability). Always read the decomposition, not just the headline number.
## Reading a Calibration Curve
Reliability has a direct visual counterpart. A **calibration curve** plots the observed event frequency against the mean predicted probability within each bin. Perfect calibration is the 45-degree diagonal: when you say 0.3, the event happens 30% of the time. Points sagging below the line mean the model is *overconfident*; points above mean it is *underconfident*. You can generate one for your own predictions with the [Calibration Curve Analysis Calculator](/calculator/calibration-curve-analysis/#src=blog-step).

# Murphy decomposition: Brier = reliability - resolution + uncertainty
murphy <- function(p, y, bins = 10) {
o_bar <- mean(y)
grp <- cut(p, breaks = seq(0, 1, length.out = bins + 1), include.lowest = TRUE)
rel <- 0; res <- 0
for (g in levels(grp)) {
idx <- grp == g
nk <- sum(idx)
if (nk == 0) next
pk <- mean(p[idx]); ok <- mean(y[idx])
rel <- rel + nk * (pk - ok)^2
res <- res + nk * (ok - o_bar)^2
}
rel <- rel / length(y); res <- res / length(y)
unc <- o_bar * (1 - o_bar)
c(brier = rel - res + unc, reliability = rel, resolution = res, uncertainty = unc)
}

## A Step-by-Step Evaluation Routine
1. **Collect aligned pairs.** Gather each predicted probability p_i and its realized outcome y_i.
2. **Compute the raw Brier score.** Average the squared errors — this is your headline number.
3. **Set a reference.** Score a naive forecaster that always predicts the base rate; the Brier Skill Score tells you how much you beat it.
4. **Decompose.** Break the score into reliability, resolution, and uncertainty to see *why* it lands where it does.
5. **Plot calibration.** Confirm the reliability term visually before trusting the model in production.
## The Brier Skill Score
A raw Brier score is hard to interpret without context, because the uncertainty term changes with the base rate. The **Brier Skill Score (BSS)** normalizes against a reference forecast (usually climatology, i.e. always predicting the base rate):
BSS = 1 - \frac{BS}{BS_{ref}}
A BSS of 1 is perfect, 0 means no improvement over the base rate, and negative means your model is worse than guessing the average. This makes scores comparable across problems with different prevalence — a key fix when an imbalanced dataset would otherwise make a useless model look impressive. Probability models such as a [Bayesian logistic regression](/docs/bayesian-logistic-regression/) benefit most from this kind of skill-relative grading.

Does a low Brier score guarantee good calibration?
No. A low Brier score reflects both calibration (reliability) and the ability to separate classes (resolution), so a model can earn a decent overall score while still being miscalibrated. To confirm calibration you should inspect the reliability term of the decomposition or plot a calibration curve rather than relying on the headline number alone.

results.title: Fourth & Value — Calibration and the Brier Score in Sports Prediction Markets
results.description:
We examine the use of proper scoring rules, specifically the Brier score, for evaluating probabilistic forecasts of NFL player performance against sportsbook betting lines. We formalize the Brier score's strict propriety, apply Murphy's (1973) three-term decomposition into reliability, resolution, and uncertainty, and compare two forecast estimators: a single-window recency estimator using each player's trailing four games, and a hierarchical shrinkage estimator that partially pools player-level estimates toward position-level priors using an empirical Bayes weighting scheme. Forecasts are evaluated out-of-sample against 12,900+ graded player-prop outcomes from the 2025 NFL season across eight statistical markets, with probability calibration fit via isotonic regression and validated under grouped cross-validation. The hierarchical estimator reduces the Brier score from 0.337 to 0.276 (reliability component: 0.086 to 0.025) relative to the single-window baseline, and reaches 0.252 after calibration — approaching the coin-flip floor of 0.25 implied by the near-even base rate of the underlying markets. We discuss the distinction between calibration and resolution, and note that a well-calibrated forecast is not equivalent to a forecast with demonstrated predictive skill.

A *proper scoring rule* corrects this by constructing a loss function under which a forecaster's expected score is optimized only by reporting their true subjective probability — no relabeling, hedging, or overstatement of confidence can improve the expected score. The Brier score [1] is the most widely used proper scoring rule for binary probabilistic forecasts and is standard in meteorology, epidemiology, and machine learning classifier calibration.

For a binary outcome o ∈ {0, 1} and a forecast probability f ∈ [0, 1] that o = 1, the Brier score over N forecast–outcome pairs is defined as:
BS = (1/N) Σi=1N (fi − oi)²(1)
The score ranges over [0, 1], with 0 indicating perfect foresight. A forecaster who reports f = 0.5 unconditionally scores exactly 0.25 regardless of the outcome sequence — the "coin-flip" reference score used throughout this note as a baseline for markets with a near-even base rate.
### 2.2 Strict Propriety
A scoring rule is *strictly proper* if, for a forecaster with true belief p, the expected score is uniquely minimized by reporting f = p. For the Brier score, the expected loss of reporting f when the true probability is p is:
E[BS] = p(1−f)² + (1−p)f²(2)
Differentiating with respect to f and setting the result to zero yields f* = p, with positive second derivative confirming a minimum. No reporting strategy other than the forecaster's true belief minimizes expected loss [2]. This property is what distinguishes the Brier score from accuracy-based metrics, which admit no such guarantee.
### 2.3 Murphy's Decomposition
Murphy (1973) [3] shows that, for forecasts grouped into K bins by predicted value, the Brier score admits an exact three-term decomposition:
BS =
(1/N) Σk nk(f̄k − ōk)² Reliability
−
(1/N) Σk nk(ōk − ō)² Resolution
+
ō(1−ō) Uncertainty
(3)
where nk is the count of forecasts in bin k, f̄k the mean forecast in that bin, ōk the observed outcome frequency in that bin, and ō the overall base rate. **Reliability** penalizes the gap between stated confidence and observed frequency (lower is better; zero indicates perfect calibration). **Resolution** rewards the forecaster for sorting cases into bins with outcome frequencies that differ from the overall base rate (higher is better; it measures discrimination, independent of calibration).

We calibrate raw forecast probabilities using isotonic regression [4], a non-parametric method that fits a monotonic step function mapping raw forecast value to empirical outcome frequency, subject to the constraint that the mapping is non-decreasing. Isotonic regression makes no assumption about the functional form of the miscalibration (unlike Platt scaling, which assumes a logistic form [5]), which is appropriate here given no prior reason to expect a particular parametric miscalibration shape.

The dominant bin (n = 7,203 of 7,236 total, 99.5% of the sample) is well calibrated (0.508 predicted vs. 0.501 observed). The small number of observations in higher-confidence bins precludes a reliable calibration estimate there; we treat this as a genuine finding about the current model's resolution rather than a defect in the calibration procedure — the model rarely produces a confidently differentiated forecast, and when it does, the sample is too small to certify that confidence out-of-sample.

We have presented a formal treatment of the Brier score as a strictly proper scoring rule, its decomposition into reliability and resolution components, and an empirical comparison of a single-window and a hierarchical shrinkage estimator for NFL player performance forecasting. The hierarchical estimator improves calibration substantially (reliability: 0.086 to 0.025) with a comparatively small change in resolution, and post-calibration performance approaches the theoretical floor implied by the near-even base rate of the underlying markets. We view continued, out-of-sample tracking of both calibration and resolution — rather than aggregate win rate — as the appropriate standard for evaluating forecasts of this kind going forward.

results.title: Comparing Probabilistic Forecasting Systems with the Brier Score
results.description:
Verification scores are commonly used as numerical summaries for the quality of weather forecasts. General introductions to forecast verification are given by Jolliffe and Stephenson (2003) and Wilks (2006, chapter 7). There are many situations in which we may wish to compare the values of a verification score computed for two sets of forecasts: to compare the quality of forecasts from a single forecasting system at different times or locations, or in different meteorological conditions, or to compare the quality of forecasts from two forecasting systems. Several authors have recommended that measures of uncertainty for the scores, such as standard errors or confidence intervals, should be computed to aid such comparisons. Woodcock (1976), Seaman et al. (1996), Kane and Brown (2000), Stephenson (2000), Thornes and Stephenson (2001), and Wilks (2006, section 7.9) propose confidence intervals for scores of deterministic binary-event forecasts. Bradley et al. (2003) use simulation to compare the biases and standard errors of different estimators for several scores of probabilistic binary-event forecasts, but do not discuss estimators for the standard errors. Hamill (1999) takes a different approach and proposes hypothesis tests for comparing the scores of two sets of deterministic or probabilistic forecasts; see also Briggs and Ruppert (2005).

We shall consider uncertainty in expected values of the Brier verification score (Brier 1950) in the case of ensemble-based probabilistic binary-event forecasts. Unbiased estimators for the expected Brier score that would be obtained for any ensemble size are defined in section 2. Standard errors and confidence intervals are developed in section 3, and their performance is assessed with a simulation study in section 4. Methods for comparing the Brier scores of two forecasting systems are presented in section 5. Confidence intervals appropriate for comparing Brier scores of two systems simultaneously for multiple events and sites are described in section 6.

We estimate the expected Brier scores B m and B ϱ for the ECMWF and MF rainfall forecasts at a range of event thresholds u and . These are shown in Fig. 2, where we set ϭ u and let u range from the 10% to the 90% quantiles of the observed rainfall. The MF forecasts appear to have significantly lower Brier scores than do those of the ECMWF for thresholds below 90 mm (about the median observed rainfall), and the two systems have similar Brier scores at higher thresholds. The estimated difference between B m for MF and B ϱ for ECMWF is also large below 90 mm, suggesting that increasing the ECMWF ensemble size would not be sufficient to match the MF Brier score.

One common reference value for B m is the Brier score, q 2 ϩ (1 Ϫ 2q)⌺I t /n, obtained if the same probability q is forecast at every time t. Another is the expected Brier score, (2m ϩ 1)/(6m) or 1/3, obtained if the forecast at each time t is selected independently from a uniform distribution on either the set {i/m : i ϭ 0, . . . , m} or the interval [0, 1].

Müller et al. (2005) have aims similar to ours but for the more general quadratic ranked probability score (RPS). They note that the expected RPS for perfectly calibrated but random ensemble forecasts exceeds the RPS obtained by forecasting climatology, which is equivalent to a perfectly calibrated random ensemble forecast with infinite ensemble size. This is analogous to B m exceeding B ϱ . Instead of using climatology as the reference forecast in RPS skill scores, they therefore propose using a perfectly calibrated random ensemble forecast with an ensemble size equal to that of the forecasts being assessed.
